subject: Chemistry
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 2-hour practical test for school candidates (1½-hour alternative to practical for private candidates) with three compulsory questions for 50 marks: one on quantitative analysis (usually an acid–base or redox titration with calculations), one on qualitative analysis (tests, observations and inferences for ions, gases and organic groups) and one on practical activities from the teaching syllabus.

practicals.title: Acid–base titration: concentration of sodium hydroxide
practicals.aim: To determine the concentration, in mol dm⁻³ and g dm⁻³, of a sodium hydroxide solution (B) by titration against a standard tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid solution (A).
materials: Solution A: H₂SO₄ containing 4.90 g dm⁻³
Solution B: NaOH of unknown concentration
safety: Always use a pipette filler — never pipette by mouth.
Wear safety goggles; acids and alkalis harm the eyes.
Remove the funnel from the burette before titrating, and fill the burette below eye level.
Wash spills on skin with plenty of water.
procedure: Rinse the burette with a little of A and fill it; run some through the jet to remove air, then record the initial reading.
Rinse the pipette with B, then pipette 25.0 cm³ of B into a clean conical flask (rinsed with distilled water only).
Add 2–3 drops of methyl orange; the solution turns yellow.
Run A from the burette into the flask with constant swirling until the colour changes from yellow to orange (end point). This first titration is the rough titre.
Repeat at least twice more, adding A rapidly to within about 1 cm³ of the rough titre, then dropwise, until you have concordant titres.
Record all readings in a table and calculate the mean of the concordant titres.
Use the mean titre and the equation H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O to calculate the concentration of B.
practicals.expectedObservations: With methyl orange the solution in the flask is yellow (alkaline) and changes sharply to orange (neutral end point) with one drop of acid; red means the end point has been overshot.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Titres: rough 25.40; accurate 24.90, 24.80, 24.85 cm³. Mean titre = (24.90 + 24.80 + 24.85)/3 = 24.85 cm³. Molar mass of H₂SO₄ = 98 g mol⁻¹, so [A] = 4.90/98 = 0.0500 mol dm⁻³. Moles of acid = 0.0500 × 24.85/1000 = 1.243 × 10⁻³ mol. Mole ratio acid : base = 1 : 2, so moles of NaOH = 2.485 × 10⁻³ mol in 25.0 cm³. [B] = 2.485 × 10⁻³ × 1000/25.0 = 0.0994 mol dm⁻³. Mass concentration = 0.0994 × 40 = 3.98 g dm⁻³.
precautions: Rinsed the burette with the acid and the pipette with the base before use; rinsed the conical flask with distilled water only.
Removed air bubbles from the burette jet.
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Swirled the flask continuously and added the titrant dropwise near the end point.
Used a white tile to see the colour change clearly.
sourcesOfError: Air bubble in the burette jet.
Drops left on the pipette tip or rinsing the flask with the base.
commonMistakes: Including the rough titre in the average.
Forgetting the 1 : 2 mole ratio of H₂SO₄ to NaOH.
Rinsing the conical flask with B (adds extra base).
Writing burette readings to one decimal place.
examTips: Record burette readings to two decimal places (e.g. 24.85 cm³) in a neat table: final, initial, volume used.
Average only concordant titres (within ±0.10 cm³ of each other); show which ones you used.
Write the balanced equation and state the mole ratio before calculating — each step earns marks.
Give answers to 3 significant figures with units (mol dm⁻³, g dm⁻³).

practicals.title: Standardising hydrochloric acid with sodium trioxocarbonate(IV)
practicals.aim: To determine the concentration of hydrochloric acid (A) by titration against a standard solution of anhydrous sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) (B).
materials: Solution A: HCl of unknown concentration
Solution B: 5.30 g dm⁻³ anhydrous Na₂CO₃
safety: Always use a pipette filler — never pipette by mouth.
Wear safety goggles; acids and alkalis harm the eyes.
Remove the funnel from the burette before titrating, and fill the burette below eye level.
Wash spills on skin with plenty of water.
procedure: Fill the burette with A after rinsing it with A; record the initial reading.
Pipette 25.0 cm³ of B into a conical flask and add 2–3 drops of methyl orange.
Titrate with A, swirling, until the yellow solution just turns orange (or pink-orange).
Do a rough titration followed by at least two accurate titrations until concordant.
Calculate the mean titre and the concentration of A using Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

[A] = 2.50 × 10⁻³ × 1000/23.50 = 0.106 mol dm⁻³; mass concentration = 0.106 × 36.5 = 3.88 g dm⁻³.
precautions: Rinsed the burette with the acid and the pipette with the base before use; rinsed the conical flask with distilled water only.
Removed air bubbles from the burette jet.
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Swirled the flask continuously and added the titrant dropwise near the end point.
Used a white tile to see the colour change clearly.

Drops left on the pipette tip or rinsing the flask with the base.

Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio.

practicals.title: Preparing a standard solution and diluting it
practicals.aim: To prepare 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) solution and to prepare a dilute solution of known concentration from it.
safety: Wear goggles.
Use a pipette filler.
procedure: Calculate the mass required: moles = 0.100 × 250/1000 = 0.0250 mol; mass = 0.0250 × 106 = 2.65 g.
Weigh about 2.65 g accurately in a weighing bottle and transfer to a beaker; reweigh the bottle to find the exact mass transferred.
Dissolve in about 100 cm³ of distilled water, stirring.
Transfer the solution through a funnel into the volumetric flask; rinse the beaker, rod and funnel several times into the flask.
Add distilled water until close to the mark, then dropwise until the bottom of the meniscus is on the mark (at eye level). Stopper and invert many times.
Dilution: pipette 25.0 cm³ of this solution into another 250 cm³ volumetric flask, make up to the mark and mix — the new concentration is ten times smaller.
practicals.expectedObservations: A clear, colourless solution. The diluted solution looks identical but is 0.0100 mol dm⁻³.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mass needed = 0.100 × 0.250 × 106 = 2.65 g. If 2.68 g was actually transferred, the true concentration = (2.68/106)/0.250 = 0.101 mol dm⁻³. Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ → 0.101 × 25.0 = C₂ × 250 → C₂ = 0.0101 mol dm⁻³. To make 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl from 1.00 mol dm⁻³ stock: V₁ = 0.100 × 250/1.00 = 25.0 cm³.
precautions: Rinsings transferred so that no solute was lost.
Meniscus brought exactly to the mark at eye level.
Flask shaken (inverted) to make the solution uniform.
Solution at room temperature before making up to the mark.
sourcesOfError: Solid left in the beaker or funnel.
commonMistakes: Dissolving the solid directly in the volumetric flask filled to the mark.
Adding 250 cm³ of water to the solid (giving a volume greater than 250 cm³).
examTips: Define a standard solution: one whose concentration is accurately known.
Show C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ for dilution questions.
List the qualities of a primary standard: pure, stable, not hygroscopic, high molar mass, soluble.

practicals.title: Iodine–thiosulphate titration
practicals.aim: To determine the concentration of iodine in a solution of iodine in potassium iodide by titration with standard sodium thiosulphate.

practicals.title: Heat of neutralisation
practicals.aim: To determine the heat (enthalpy) of neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide.
safety: Wear safety goggles throughout.
NaOH is corrosive — wash skin splashes at once.
procedure: Measure 50.0 cm³ of the acid into the polystyrene cup placed in a beaker for support. Record its steady temperature.
Measure 50.0 cm³ of NaOH into a cylinder and record its temperature (it should be the same; otherwise use the average as the initial temperature).
Pour the alkali quickly into the acid, cover, stir with the thermometer and record the highest temperature reached.
Calculate the heat given out with Q = mcΔT (take the mixture as 100 g with c = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹) and divide by the moles of water formed.
practicals.expectedObservations: The temperature rises by several degrees; the cup feels warm — the reaction is exothermic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Initial temperature 28.0 °C; highest 34.7 °C; ΔT = 6.7 K. Q = 100 × 4.2 × 6.7 = 2814 J. Moles of water = 0.0500 (50.0 cm³ × 1.00 mol dm⁻³). ΔH = −2814/0.0500 = −56 300 J mol⁻¹ = −56.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (accepted about −57 kJ mol⁻¹).
precautions: Used a polystyrene cup with a lid to reduce heat loss.
Mixed quickly and stirred.
Recorded the highest steady temperature.
Ensured both solutions started at the same temperature.

practicals.aim: To separate the components of an ink or food colouring by paper chromatography and calculate their Rf values.
apparatus: Beaker or gas jar with lid
materials: Black ink or felt-tip pen ink
Pure food dyes A and B
safety: Ethanol is flammable — keep away from flames.
procedure: Draw a pencil base line 1.5 cm from the bottom of the paper.
Spot the ink and the pure dyes on the line with a capillary tube; let each dry and re-spot to concentrate.
Stand the paper in the solvent so that the solvent level is below the base line; cover the container.
When the solvent has risen near the top, remove the paper, mark the solvent front with pencil and dry.
Measure the distance moved by each spot and by the solvent; calculate Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.

Solvent level below the spots.
Container covered to keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent.
Small, concentrated spots used.

Letting the solvent touch the spots directly.
examTips: Rf has no unit and is always less than 1.
Applications: detecting food colourings, drugs, checking purity, separating plant pigments (chlorophyll from bitter leaf or green leaves).

practicals.title: Purification by recrystallisation and melting-point test
practicals.aim: To purify impure benzoic acid by recrystallisation from hot water and check purity by melting point.
materials: Impure benzoic acid (with sand or charcoal)
safety: Wear safety goggles throughout.
Hot oil baths cause severe burns — heat slowly and do not overheat.
Benzoic acid dust irritates — avoid inhaling.
procedure: Weigh 5.00 g of impure benzoic acid and dissolve it in the minimum volume of boiling water.
Filter the hot solution quickly through a warmed funnel to remove insoluble impurities.
Cool the filtrate slowly, then in ice, to form crystals.
Filter off the crystals, wash with a little ice-cold water, dry and weigh.
Pack a little dry sample into a capillary tube sealed at one end, attach it to the thermometer and heat slowly in the oil bath; record the temperature range over which it melts.
practicals.expectedObservations: White needle-like crystals form on cooling. Pure benzoic acid melts sharply at about 122 °C; the impure sample melts lower and over a wider range.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Mass of impure sample = 5.00 g; mass of dry recrystallised acid = 4.10 g. Percentage recovery = 4.10/5.00 × 100 = 82.0%. Melting range: impure 115–119 °C; recrystallised 121–122 °C (literature 122 °C).
precautions: Used the minimum amount of hot solvent.
Cooled slowly for larger, purer crystals.
Heated the oil bath slowly near the melting point.
Crystals fully dry before weighing.
sourcesOfError: Product lost in the filtrate (some is soluble even when cold).
Crystallisation in the funnel during hot filtration.
commonMistakes: Using too much water, giving a poor yield.
Heating the melting-point tube too fast and recording a high value.
examTips: A pure substance has a sharp melting point; impurities lower it and broaden the range.
Recrystallisation works because solubility is much higher in hot solvent than in cold.

practicals.title: Laboratory preparation and properties of ammonia
practicals.aim: To prepare ammonia from an ammonium salt and an alkali, dry and collect it, and demonstrate its properties.
apparatus: Hard-glass test tube or round-bottom flask with bung and delivery tube
materials: Concentrated HCl on a glass rod
safety: Wear safety goggles throughout.
Ammonia irritates eyes and lungs — prepare in a fume cupboard or near an open window.
Clamp the tube sloping downwards so condensed water does not run back on to the hot glass.
procedure: Mix NH₄Cl and Ca(OH)₂ (about 1 : 1 by mass) and put the mixture in the tube clamped with its mouth slightly downwards.
Heat gently; pass the gas through a tower of quicklime to dry it.
Collect the gas by upward delivery (downward displacement of air) in an inverted gas jar, since ammonia is lighter than air.
Test with damp red litmus at the mouth of the jar and with a rod dipped in conc. HCl.
Demonstrate high solubility with the fountain experiment.
practicals.expectedObservations: A colourless gas with a pungent smell turns damp red litmus blue and forms dense white fumes (NH₄Cl) with HCl. In the fountain experiment, water rushes into the flask and turns pink with phenolphthalein.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃. 5.35 g NH₄Cl (M = 53.5) = 0.100 mol → 0.100 mol NH₃ = 0.100 × 24.0 = 2.40 dm³ at r.t.p. Ca(OH)₂ needed = 0.0500 mol × 74 = 3.70 g.
precautions: Dried with quicklime (not conc. H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂, which react with NH₃).
Tube sloping downward.
Collected by upward delivery.
commonMistakes: Collecting ammonia over water (it is very soluble).
Drying with conc. H₂SO₄.
examTips: Uses of ammonia: fertilisers (urea, NH₄NO₃), Haber process, cleaning agents.
